claims.text: Every request to the API server passes authentication, then authorization, then admission controllers (for requests that create, change or delete objects) before the object is stored in etcd.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Concepts > Security > Controlling Access to the Kubernetes API (Authentication, Authorization, Admission control)

claims.text: Kubernetes has no objects for normal user accounts (people); a user is the name carried by a credential the API server trusts. A client certificate, presented by the client over TLS, names the user and its groups inside itself.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Reference > API Access Control > Authenticating (Users in Kubernetes; X509 client certificates: CN = user, O = groups)

claims.text: A credential the API server cannot verify is rejected with 401 before authorization runs; kubectl prints 'error: You must be logged in to the server (Unauthorized)'. --insecure-skip-tls-verify only skips checking the server's certificate.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Authenticating (rejected with HTTP 401); outputs/stage-3/scripts/k8s/api-request-checks.txt; kubectl global flags (--insecure-skip-tls-verify)

claims.text: Authorization decides from request attributes only: user and groups, verb, resource and API group, namespace, and the name when the request names one object; never the object's fields. A rule may allow a group. Pods are in the core API group, shown as "". Denied: 403.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Reference > API Access Control > Authorization (Review your request attributes; Determine the request verb)

claims.text: Admission controllers apply to create, modify and delete requests, not reads (get, watch, list); they see the object, mutating ones may change it, and any one can reject the request so nothing is persisted.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Reference > API Access Control > Admission Control in Kubernetes (What are they?; Admission control phases: mutating, validating; any rejection rejects the request)

claims.text: kubectl auth whoami prints the attributes the API server assigned to the caller; on donhang-staging, kind's kubeconfig signs in as kubernetes-admin in groups kubeadm:cluster-admins and system:authenticated.
Every authenticated caller is added to the group system:authenticated.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Authenticating (Authentication strategies: system:authenticated added to all authenticated users)

claims.text: kubectl auth can-i checks whether an action is allowed (authorization only, via SelfSubjectAccessReview) and creates nothing; it prints yes or no.
claims.source_hint: kubectl reference: auth can-i; kubernetes.io Authorization (Checking API access)

claims.text: With --as, kubectl acts as another user (impersonation); the API server allows it only if the real caller may impersonate users, which kubernetes-admin may. The impersonated name need not exist anywhere in the cluster.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Authenticating > User impersonation; kubectl global flag --as

claims.text: The 403 message from kubectl names user, verb, resource, API group and namespace: 'Error from server (Forbidden): pods is forbidden: User "junior-dev" cannot list resource "pods" in API group "" in the namespace "security-lessons"'.

claims.text: Opinion: read the order into errors: a 401 says nothing about rights, a 403 nothing about what the object contains.
kubectl get <resource> without a name is a list request (authorization verb list); get is the verb for reading one named object, as the 403 line for kubectl get pods shows.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Authorization (Determine the request verb: GET on a collection = list, on one resource = get); outputs/stage-3/scripts/k8s/api-request-checks.txt
